routes.description: Establish that Paul understood Jesus as an earthly historical person by combining Pauline biographical and familial references with an earthly reading of the crucifying rulers and corroboration from sources connected to Paul and the Gospel tradition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the Pauline references are best explained as ordinary historical claims, the rulers passage situates the crucifixion among human authorities, and the proposed Acts and Gospel corroboration remains sufficiently independent and reliable to reinforce that reading.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative evidence is better explained by Paul referring to a human Jesus who lived and was crucified on Earth than by a wholly celestial setting for the saving events.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline references to ancestry, birth, teachings, associates, betrayal, and execution supply meaningful historical particularity.
Establish from the context of First Corinthians that the rulers responsible for the crucifixion are human authorities, even if spiritual forces also participated.
Show that references to James and other brothers of the Lord are most coherently understood as biological relationships to Jesus.
Establish that Acts is substantially reliable and connected to a companion of Paul, making its historical Jesus relevant to reconstructing Paul's understanding.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend a sufficiently broad Pauline corpus so that relevant historical references are not excluded solely by disputed authorship judgments.
Show that dispersed incidental correspondences among Gospel narratives are more expected on historical information than deliberate literary harmonization.

routes.description: Establish that Paul's accepted letters do not securely locate Jesus's ministry, death, and resurrection on Earth, while their cosmic language permits a flesh-bearing celestial figure killed by demonic rulers in a mythic heavenly realm.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Pauline biographical and familial expressions remain materially ambiguous, the rulers and cosmology make a heavenly crucifixion viable, and Acts and Gospel narratives cannot independently import a later earthly biography into Paul's letters.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest relevant Pauline evidence remains compatible with, and materially supports, a mortal embodied Jesus whose death and resurrection occurred in a celestial rather than terrestrial realm.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the accepted Pauline letters lack an unambiguous earthly ministry or terrestrial location for Jesus's death and resurrection.
Show that the rulers of the age can be celestial demonic powers and that their concealed knowledge and interests fit that interpretation.
Establish that ancient cosmology allowed heavenly counterparts of earthly places, objects, and practices, making a celestial crucifixion intelligible.
Show that Acts and the Gospels are too disputed, literary, dependent, or historically unstable to determine what Paul believed about Jesus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that Pauline brother-of-the-Lord language can identify an ordinary baptized Christian rather than a biological sibling of Jesus.
Supply the comparative possibility that a savior cult could later place a nonhistorical divine figure into an earthly narrative.

sections.title: Pauline Biography, Silence, and Corpus Scope
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether the relevant Pauline letters contain historical markers sufficient to locate Jesus on Earth, and whether the admissible Pauline corpus expands or restricts that evidence.

sections.title: The Rulers and the Realm of Crucifixion
sections.rationale: The identity of the rulers of the age and the cosmological intelligibility of heavenly counterparts directly distinguish an earthly execution by human authorities from a celestial passion involving demonic powers.

sections.title: James and the Brothers of the Lord
sections.rationale: Whether Paul's references identify biological relatives or members of a baptized cultic family is among the most direct disputes over historical particularity within the Pauline evidence.

sections.title: Acts, Pauline Chronology, and Companion Authorship
sections.rationale: Acts can connect Paul to a thoroughly historical Jesus only if its chronology, factual reliability, first-person narration, and claimed relationship to a Pauline companion survive the competing literary explanation.

sections.title: Gospel Independence and Undesigned Coincidences
sections.rationale: The evidential value of cross-Gospel correspondences depends on whether dispersed details reflect independent historical information or deliberate adaptation and harmonization of earlier narrative sources.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Carrier's mythicist thesis grants that Paul conceived Jesus as acquiring mortal Jewish flesh while locating his death and resurrection in a mythic realm rather than on Earth.
moves.attributionBasis: The proposition occurs within Carrier's uninterrupted thesis-setting turn after the moderator explicitly invites him to present his position.

response.rationale: Constructively defines the celestial thesis while expressly granting mortal Jewish embodiment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Clear thesis-setting contact with the motion bridge, though comparative support is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable and expressly qualified, but “mythic realm” is not closely specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It states what the thesis holds with appropriate certainty, though the comparative analogy is only sketched.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The embodied-yet-celestial position is internally intelligible, with the realm mechanics left for later support.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt clearly establishes the thesis but only gestures toward a parallel savior cult.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly states the con motion-level account.

representationalCharity.rationale: This move defines Carrier's own thesis rather than evaluating a live alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier expressly grants flesh, blood, Jewish identity, mortality, death, and resurrection while denying an earthly or Jerusalem setting.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The seven accepted Pauline letters do not locate Jesus's life and death on Earth or describe an earthly ministry, while presenting his teachings as received through revelation.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier remains the sole speaker throughout the passage and explicitly turns from comparative religion to the evidentiary contents of Paul's letters.

response.rationale: Constructively argues from the accepted letters' alleged lack of terrestrial biography and their revelatory presentation of teachings.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Direct, sustained construction of a central evidentiary bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clear, but broad negatives such as never mentioning anything on Earth require qualifications for indirect or disputed references.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Categorical silence claims exceed what the listed examples alone establish.

charity.decisiveQualification: The move must distinguish absence of a narrated ministry from absence of all terrestrial implications.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The silence inference is coherent, but it compresses the bridge from omitted biography to celestial location.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete omissions support the claim, while contrary Pauline markers and the inference from silence remain untreated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central terrestrial-silence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It presents meaningful silence evidence but does not address the strongest indirect-marker interpretation.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The restriction of Pauline evidence to seven letters rests on a contestable authorship consensus, and the case for treating all thirteen letters as Pauline should be reconsidered.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the discussion to McLatchie, who identifies Carrier by name, cites Carrier's methodological concern, and states his contrary authorship position.

components.text: Challenges the restriction of relevant Pauline evidence to seven accepted letters.
Must positively warrant treating all thirteen letters as Pauline.

response.rationale: It contacts the corpus restriction but supplies little positive authorship analysis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A partial answer: it attacks the scope premise but leaves the decisive positive authorship warrant underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The disagreement is clear, with an implicit rather than explicit distinction between contesting consensus formation and proving authorship.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The call for reconsideration is moderate, but the quotation does not itself establish thirteen-letter authenticity.

charity.alternative: A flawed consensus process can still reach correct letter-by-letter authorship conclusions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Process criticism must be supplemented by positive authorship evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from a disputed consensus process to reconsideration is valid but does not establish the desired corpus.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the subsidiary corpus-scope bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly identifies methodological contestability but does not confront this decisive distinction.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Paul's letters contain multiple historical markers for Jesus, including Davidic descent, birth from a woman under the law, teachings, brothers, followers, betrayal, a final meal, and crucifixion by rulers.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie continues his identified response and expressly introduces information he says can be extracted about Jesus's life from the Pauline epistles.

components.text: Supplies Pauline references offered as counterexamples to alleged terrestrial silence.
Must show that these markers favor an earthly setting over a flesh-bearing celestial interpretation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cumulative list has force, but several interpretations and authorship assumptions are not qualified.

charity.alternative: These references may be revelatory, cultic, scriptural, or compatible with a celestial embodied Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must compare those readings rather than merely enumerate references.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple markers can cumulatively answer silence, but the bridge from each reference to terrestrial biography is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific passages are named, while authenticity, translation, and rival readings are largely undefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the central Pauline-biographical-markers bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It offers genuine counterevidence but omits the strongest rival interpretations.

moves.evidenceBasis: McLatchie cites birth under law, Pilate, teachings, betrayal, a final meal, brothers, twelve followers, and crucifying rulers.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Paul's rulers of this age can be demonic powers, whose hostile motives and ignorance of God's concealed salvific plan fit the crucifixion passage better than obedient earthly authorities.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie explicitly yields the cited passage to Carrier, whose ensuing uninterrupted turn analyzes the Greek terminology and contrasts possible agents of the crucifixion.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier contrasts hostile crucifiers with Romans 13 authorities and links their ignorance to God's concealed cosmic plan.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Ancient Jewish cosmology could place counterparts of earthly objects and practices in heavenly realms, making a celestial counterpart of crucifixion intelligible within that worldview.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier answers the moderator's direct objection by invoking Hebrews and the Ascension of Isaiah during a clearly bounded uninterrupted response.

moves.proposition: The surrounding contrast between divine wisdom and ordinary human wisdom indicates that the rulers who crucified Jesus in First Corinthians are human authorities rather than exclusively demonic forces.

Directly locates the crucifixion on Earth rather than in a heavenly counterpart.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Richard by name, and the ensuing extended answer presents Carrier's book-based grammatical and contextual interpretation.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly returns to Richard, whose answer addresses both the Pauline passage and McLatchie's appeal to later narrative sources.

Challenges use of brother references as Pauline terrestrial markers.

moves.proposition: Acts is an agenda-driven work of fictionalized history that may reshape source material so extensively that historical facts cannot reliably be separated from its narrative embellishments.

moves.proposition: Undesigned correspondences between Paul's letters and Acts support Acts's substantial historical accuracy and the identification of its author as Paul's traveling companion Luke.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The feeding narrative's relevant facts are dispersed across John and Luke in a way that deliberate harmonization should have made explicit, favoring an undesigned coincidence.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator asks Jonathan why deliberate reconciliation is insufficient, this answer returns specifically to his feeding-of-the-five-thousand example.

components.text: Argues that the relevant facts are too dispersed across chapters and Gospels to look like explicit harmonization.
Addresses later-source contradiction evidence outside the Gospels.

response.rationale: It directly challenges the designed-harmonization explanation for the feeding example.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A direct answer to the dependence explanation, though it does not quantify why dispersal is unlikely under literary composition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The locations of the details and the dispersal inference are clearly stated, with intentionality only implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Dispersal supports the inference but does not by itself establish undesigned origin.

charity.alternative: An author who knows source characters and locations need not restate every associated fact in the adapted scene.
charity.decisiveQualification: Implicit source use can naturally produce dispersed rather than explicit correspondences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Dispersal is relevant to design, but the inference that design should be explicit is not fully warranted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific chapter locations support the factual pattern, while the probabilistic literary warrant remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the subsidiary Gospel-coincidences bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move emphasizes non-explicitness but does not answer this compositional mechanism.

moves.evidenceBasis: McLatchie notes that John 6 omits Bethsaida and places Philip and Andrew's origins elsewhere, while Luke supplies the location.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: An author adapting earlier Gospel material can select characters found in those sources without restating every associated location, naturally producing the alleged feeding-narrative coincidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier immediately answers McLatchie's hidden-coincidence challenge and explains the author's character selection through conscious use of sources.

components.text: Explains selection of Philip from source material without requiring restatement of every location detail.
Provides a general literary mechanism for the broader coincidence argument.

response.rationale: It directly answers the feeding example and applies the same mechanism to the broader inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Explicitly contacts the decisive inference from dispersed facts to undesigned coincidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-selection mechanism is clear, but “exactly that kind of reasoning” is generalized without specifying documentary examples.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The mechanism is plausible, but the move asserts that this is what occurred without passage-level evidence sufficient to exclude coincidence or tradition.

charity.alternative: The selected characters may derive from independent memory or tradition, and the dispersed fit may remain unintended.
charity.decisiveQualification: A possible literary mechanism is not evidence that this author used it in this passage.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Character selection from known sources coherently explains why associated location facts need not be repeated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposed mechanism is realistic but is asserted without direct textual indicators or representative compositional parallels.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly attacks the subsidiary Gospel-coincidences bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explains the rival possibility but treats it as established rather than comparing alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier describes an adapting author choosing Philip from available source characters without repeating all associated information.
